messages.subject: Syntax error in (relatively) simple multinomial logit model
parts:
I am trying to run a multinomial logisticregression with ~21K observations, 4 predictors (for now), and 4 alternative outcomes. The data matrix includes a column of ones to estimate the intercepts. The following code is the same as in Sec 5.5 of the manual, plus my attempt to constrain coefficients for the first alternative (K=1) to be zero (per top p. 43 in the manual):


data {
  int<lower=2> K;   # alternatives
  int<lower=0> N;   # observations
  int<lower=1> D;   # variables
  int<lower=1,upper=K> y[N];    # outcome indicator
  vector[K] xmat[N];   # matrix of x variables with 1 in first column
}
  
parameters {
  matrix[K,D] beta;
}

model {
  for (d in 1:D)
    beta[1,d] <- 0;
  for (k in 2:K)
    for (d in 1:D)
      beta[k,d] ~ normal(0,2);
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ categorical(softmax(b0 + beta * xmat[n]));
}

The syntax error message says that the assignment statement "beta[1,d] <- 0" is in the wrong block. Is this the appropriate way to constrain the coefficients for K=1? If so, where should the prodigal statement go? If not, what would work?

NB: This model runs fine when xmat does not include a column of ones and all coefficients are unconstrained. But I need intercepts because I'm sneaking up on a multilevel model with random intercepts.

parameters {

matrix[K,D-1] beta_free;
}

model {
  matrix[K,D] beta;
  beta <- append_col(rep_vector(0, K), beta_free);
  to_vector(beta_free) ~ normal(0,2);
for (n in 1:N)

y[n] ~ categorical(softmax(beta * xmat[n]));
}

Ben

parts:
I added a note to the latest manual issue to fix the doc.

The to_vector is just because we don't allow matrix arguments
to univariate densities because of issues in trying to interpret
what matching shapes mean. If there is more than one vector or
container argument, they all must be the same size.

The problem you're having is that all the dimensions have to line
up.

Problem 1: You're trying to initialize K x D and you only
want to initialize (K-1) x D, because you initialize the parameter,
not the transformed thing.

Problem 2: beta * xmat[n] dimensions won't line up, because
beta is K x D and xmat[n] is K x 1. We don't test sizes at
compile time, which is why the model compiles. What you want
is to declare xmat as an array of row vectors and use

xmat[n] * beta

or you want to declare beta as being D x K instead of D x K
and fix everything else.

Problem 3: You don't want to apply softmax directly. Use
the appropriate categorical, which is more efficient and
arithmetically stable,

y[n] ~ categorical_logit(xmat[n] * beta);

Then you can vectorize and if xmat is declared as a matrix,
just use

y ~ categorical_logit(xmat * beta);

which is the most stable and efficient way to code this.

Problem 4: Did you want to append a row of 1 rather than 0? The
row of 0 isn't going to do much in a multiplication. Also, it's
inefficient to do it this way as opposed to the way you originally wrote it.

- Bob

parts: Thanks for all assistance. The model now runs beautifully--with ~22K observations, 8 predictors, and 4 categorical outcomes, it converges in < 50 iterations, which seems pretty amazing, and it runs at a little under a second per iteration. So it takes about 15 minutes to generate about 1000 samples (3 chains, 50/350). You are welcome to use (and edit) the code as an example, for what it's worth:

data {
  int<lower=2> C;   # categories of y
  int<lower=0> N;   # observations
  int<lower=1> K;   # variables
  int<lower=1,upper=C> y[N];    # outcome indicator

vector[K] xmat[N];
}
  
parameters {
  matrix[C-1,K] beta_free;
}

transformed parameters {
  matrix[C,K] beta;
  for (k in 1:K)
    beta[1,k] <- 0;
  for (c in 2:C)
    for (k in 1:K)
      beta[c,k] <- beta_free[c-1,k];
}

model {
  for (c in 2:C)
    for (k in 1:K)
      beta[c,k] ~ normal(0,2);

for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ categorical(softmax(beta * xmat[n]));
}

You'll note that I borrowed from the Alligators example to constrain parameters for the first outcome to be zero.

Best,
John

messages.subject: comment on #warmup iterations needed
parts:
I recommend doing half the iterations for warmup and half for samples that you use. Economizing on warmup isn’t always such an economy. Or, to put it another way: If you only need 50 warmup, I think you probably only need 50 for samples. Or, if you want to be safe and have 350 for samples, I think you should really be safe and have 350 for warmup.

I have no proof on this (it’s an issue I’ve thought about, without success, for about 25 years) but that’s my impression.
A

P.S. I’m glad the model runs beautifully!

I am trying to run a multinomial logisticregression with ~21K observations, 4 predictors (for now), and 4 alternative outcomes. The data matrix includes a column of ones to estimate the intercepts. The following code is the same as in Sec 5.5 of the manual, plus my attempt to constrain coefficients for the first alternative (K=1) to be zero (per top p. 43 in the manual):


data {
  int<lower=2> K;   # alternatives
  int<lower=0> N;   # observations
  int<lower=1> D;   # variables
  int<lower=1,upper=K> y[N];    # outcome indicator
  vector[K] xmat[N];   # matrix of x variables with 1 in first column
}
  
parameters {
  matrix[K,D] beta;
}

model {
  for (d in 1:D)
    beta[1,d] <- 0;
  for (k in 2:K)
    for (d in 1:D)
      beta[k,d] ~ normal(0,2);
  for (n in 1:N)
    y[n] ~ categorical(softmax(b0 + beta * xmat[n]));
}

The syntax error message says that the assignment statement "beta[1,d] <- 0" is in the wrong block. Is this the appropriate way to constrain the coefficients for K=1? If so, where should the prodigal statement go? If not, what would work?

NB: This model runs fine when xmat does not include a column of ones and all coefficients are unconstrained. But I need intercepts because I'm sneaking up on a multilevel model with random intercepts.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Syntax error in (relatively) simple multinomial logit model
parts:
I missed this the first time around, but to answer your efficiency issues,
see below.

Change this:

for (c in 1:C){
for (j in 1:J){

eb0[c,j] <- z[j] * b0[c];
}

to

for (c in 1:C)
eb0[c] <- z * b0[c];

It'll vectorize the scalar multiplications. And change this

for (c in 1:C){
for (j in 1:J){

a0[c,j] ~ normal(eb0[c,j], sigma[c]);
}
}

to

for (c in 1:C)
a0[c] ~ normal(eb0[c], sigma[c]);

That'll be a big win. As will be changing this

for (c in 1:C){
b0[c] ~ normal(0, 10);
}

to

b0 ~ normal(0, 10);

Finally, change this:

for ( i in 1:N ) {
for (c in 1:C){
s[i,c] <- a0[c,id[i]] + x[i] * b[c] ;
theta[1] <- 0;
theta[c+1] <- s[i,c];
}
y[i] ~ categorical_logit(theta);
}

to

theta[1] <- 0;
for (n in 1:N)

theta[2:C] <- a0[1:C, id[i]] + x[i] * b;
y[n] ~ categorical_logit(theta);
}

I only looked at the first file, but hopefully you see the pattern.

- Bob
